result.summary: Aeneas passes Parthenope and reaches Cumae, where the Sibyl agrees to guide him through Avernus to his father's shade. On the return he thanks her as a goddess, and she explains that she is mortal, cursed with long life without youth because of her bargain with Phoebus.

scenes.title: Aeneas Seeks the Sibyl
scenes.summary: Aeneas reaches Cumae and asks the Sibyl to lead him to his father. She promises, points out the golden branch, and he sees the underworld and Anchises.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas risks the dangers of the underworld and needs the Sibyl's guidance to reach his father's shade.

scenes.title: Return and Offer of Worship
scenes.summary: Returning from the dead, Aeneas praises the Sibyl and promises her a temple and incense. She refuses, saying she is no goddess.
scenes.stakes: The Sibyl wishes to correct a mistaken belief about her nature.

scenes.title: The Sibyl's Tale of Phoebus
scenes.summary: The Sibyl tells how she asked Phoebus for years as many as grains of dust but forgot youth, and refused him. She faces shrinking old age, remembered only by her voice.
scenes.stakes: She suffers endless decay, losing her beauty and being forgotten, with only her voice left.

characters.name: Sibyl
characters.description: long-lived prophetess of Cumae who guides Aeneas

characters.name: Apollo
characters.description: god who loved the Sibyl and offered her a gift

alias_notes.explanation: Phœbus is a title of Apollo, used in the Sibyl's speech.
Apollo addresses the Sibyl by her home town.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable maxim that virtue finds every path open.
Poignant close: only her voice will survive her withering.

analysis.text: The Sibyl's story shows how a careless wish brings suffering: she gains endless time without youth. It links Aeneas's epic journey to Ovid's themes of desire and change.
Ovid retells Virgil's Aeneid book 6 briefly and adds his own tale of the Cumaean Sibyl, a famous Roman prophetic figure.

legacy.text: T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) opens with an epigraph from Petronius about the Sibyl hanging in a jar and wishing to die, drawing on her legend.

fun_facts.text: The Sibyl's cave at Cumae, a trapezoidal tunnel near Lake Avernus, is a visitable archaeological site identified with her legend.

language_notes.text: Parthenope is an old name for Naples; the tomb is that of Misenus, Aeneas's trumpeter, son of Æolus, buried on the headland later called Misenum.
Avernus is a volcanic lake near Cumæ, believed to be an entrance to the underworld.
"Proved by the flames" refers to Aeneas's devotion in carrying his father out of burning Troy.
The "Juno of Avernus" is Proserpine, queen of the underworld, to whom the golden bough was sacred; it served as the pass into her realm.
Orcus is a Roman name for the underworld and its god of the dead.
The second "abodes of death" clause is awkwardly worded: he thanks her for letting him enter the underworld and also return from it.
"Maiden of Cumæ" refers to the Sibyl, the prophetess who lived at Cumæ, near Naples, in Italy.
"Inconsiderately" means thoughtlessly, without thinking through what she was asking for.
"Seven ages" means seven generations, about 700 years. The Sibyl counts her years by harvests and vintages, each marking one year.
"Diminutive" means very small; she will shrink from the large woman she once was.
The Destinies (the Fates) are the goddesses who control the length and course of human life.

context_notes.text: Apollo's offer and the Sibyl's blunder explain her great age; in the wider legend she shrivels until only her voice remains.
Anchises, Aeneas's father, died in Sicily; in the underworld he shows his son the future of Rome.
Phœbus is Apollo; the Sibyl was granted long life but refused his love, so she never received eternal youth.
Phoebus is Apollo, god of prophecy, music and the sun. He offered the Sibyl a gift in return for her love.
Her refusal of the god explains why she gained long life without lasting youth.

literary_notes.text: The Sibyl's prophetic trance, with her gaze fixed on the ground until the god inspires her, presents her as a true vessel of Apollo.
The Sibyl condenses her encouragement into a general maxim, giving her prophecy a solemn, proverbial authority.
Aeneas's claim that he owes his very existence to her exaggerates his gratitude and sets up her refusal of divine honors.
Aeneas offers worship to one who is not divine and who is, tragically, burdened by the gift she once sought from a god.
Her wish is granted exactly as she phrased it, and the one thing she forgot to ask for makes the gift a curse.
Old age is made a creature that approaches with a trembling step, which makes its coming seem slow and inevitable.
The repeated "nor once" stresses how completely her past beauty and divine favor will be forgotten.
The brief closing line anticipates her fate: only her voice will survive when her body has withered away.
